\chapter{Counting Past Your Fingers}
\label{ch:cien-y-la-cantidad}
\hlchaptermodality{351}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say cien, la cantidad, ambos, varios and el triple, and say why cien and English hundred are the same word split by one sound change.}

Complete ES-C351-triple: count to a hundred, name an amount, take two together, say there are several, and treble a figure.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cien]{cien — a hundred, and the \emph{hundred} hiding in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C351-cien}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a different one}, then \emph{the kind}. (\emph{Distinto}; \emph{el tipo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item veinte — the biggest number you had until now.
  \item mucho · muy, malo · mal — the same tail-cutting at work.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SIEN}, one beat. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft, and \emph{ie} is a single glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cien} — \textquotedblleft{}a hundred.\textquotedblright{}

The full word is \textbf{ciento}, and Spanish cuts the tail off before a noun: \textbf{cien libros}, a hundred books. That is the same trick you have already met with \emph{mucho} going to \emph{muy} and \emph{malo} going to \emph{mal}.

Latin \textbf{centum} is the source, and it turns up all over English: a \textbf{cent} is a hundredth, a \textbf{century} is a hundred years, a \textbf{centipede} is a hundred-foot, a \textbf{centurion} commanded a hundred men, and \textbf{percent} is \emph{by the hundred}.

Now the good part. English \textbf{hundred} is the same ancient word. The line that became Latin kept the sound at the front as a \emph{c}; the line that became English turned that \emph{c} into an \emph{h}, all the way down the vocabulary — which is also why Latin \emph{cornu} matches English \textbf{horn} and Latin \emph{cord-} matches \textbf{heart}.

So \textbf{cien} and \textbf{hundred} are one word, separated by a single sound change, several thousand years ago.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A number bigger than your fingers, and a rule for shortening it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cien}
  \item \emph{cien libros}
  \item \emph{cien días}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the full form of \emph{cien}? (\emph{Ciento}.) And which plain English number is the same ancient word? (Hundred.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cantidad]{la cantidad — the amount, from a question word}

\label{lesson:ES-C351-cantidad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the kind}, then \emph{a hundred}. (\emph{El tipo}; \emph{cien}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mucho — a rough answer to the question this asks.
  \item poco — the other rough answer.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kan-ti-DAD}, three beats with the weight on the last. The final \emph{d} is very soft, close to a breath. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cantidad} — \textquotedblleft{}the quantity,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the amount.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{quantus} is a question: \emph{how much?} Make a noun of it with \textbf{-tātem} and you get \textbf{quantitās}, \emph{how-much-ness} — the answer treated as a thing.

Spanish has done this to you already. That \textbf{-tātem} is the \textbf{-dad} on the end of \emph{verdad}, \emph{ciudad} and \emph{edad}. Once you spot it, you can hear a Latin abstract noun coming a long way off.

English took the same word twice. \textbf{Quantity} through French, worn smooth. And \textbf{quantum} straight out of Latin, meaning \emph{how much there is of a thing} — which is why the smallest indivisible amount of energy got that name. \textbf{Quantify} and \textbf{quantitative} follow.

\emph{Cantidad} is the neutral word. It carries no judgement about whether the amount is big or small; that is what \emph{mucho} and \emph{poco} are for.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A noun for the answer to \emph{how much}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cantidad}
  \item \emph{una cantidad grande}
  \item \emph{la cantidad de libros}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{quantus} ask? (How much.) And which Spanish ending is Latin \emph{-tātem}? (\emph{-dad}, as in \emph{verdad} and \emph{ciudad}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ambos]{ambos — both, and the two sides of \emph{ambiguous}}

\label{lesson:ES-C351-ambos}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a hundred}, then \emph{the amount}. (\emph{Cien}; \emph{la cantidad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — the two this gathers.
  \item unos · unas — the vaguer handful.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{AM-bos}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{b} after \emph{m} is a full \emph{b}, not the soft one between vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ambos} — \textquotedblleft{}both.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish can say \emph{los dos}. \textbf{Ambos} is the tighter word: the two of them, taken together as a pair rather than counted one after the other.

Latin \textbf{ambō} is that pair, and the \textbf{amb-} at its front is an old piece meaning \emph{on both sides, round about}.

English is full of it and rarely notices. \textbf{Ambidextrous} is having a right hand on both sides. \textbf{Ambiguous} is a phrase that drives both ways at once — the \emph{-ig-} is \emph{agere}, to drive. \textbf{Ambition} was going round on both sides of a crowd asking for votes. \textbf{Ambient} is what goes round about you.

Greek had the same piece as \textbf{amphí}, which gives \textbf{amphitheatre}, a theatre with seats on both sides, and an \textbf{amphibian}, which lives both lives.

\emph{Ambos} agrees like any adjective: \textbf{ambos libros}, \textbf{ambas casas}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for two things held as one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ambos}
  \item \emph{ambos libros}
  \item \emph{ambas casas}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the piece \emph{amb-} mean? (On both sides, round about.) And what is an \textbf{amphibian}, word for word? (A thing that lives both lives.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[varios]{varios — several, and the speckled hide behind it}

\label{lesson:ES-C351-varios}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the amount}, then \emph{both}. (\emph{La cantidad}; \emph{ambos}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item poco — fewer than this.
  \item bastante — more than this.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BA-rios}, with a first syllable \emph{va-} made with both lips, and the weight on it. \emph{-rios} is one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{varios} — \textquotedblleft{}several,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a few of different sorts.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{varius} did not mean \emph{several}. It meant \textbf{speckled} — a hide with blotches on it, a sky of broken cloud, marble with veins running through.

From mottled came \emph{mixed}, from mixed came \emph{of more than one kind}, and only then came the plain plural sense Spanish uses now. So \emph{varios libros} is not merely \emph{some books}; underneath, it is \emph{books that are not all the same}.

English kept every step. \textbf{Variegated} leaves are the speckled ones, right back at the start. \textbf{Variety} is a mixture. To \textbf{vary} is to become mottled with change. \textbf{Various} and \textbf{variance} finish the family.

You will hear it in front of its noun, agreeing with it: \textbf{varias casas}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four counting words, and each one a different way of not saying a number.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{varios}
  \item \emph{varios libros}
  \item \emph{varias casas}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{varius} mean first? (Speckled, blotched.) And which English word for leaves keeps that sense? (Variegated.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el triple]{el triple — three times over, and the fold in \emph{simple}}

\label{lesson:ES-C351-triple}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{both}, then \emph{several}. (\emph{Ambos}; \emph{varios}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — the \emph{three} inside it.
  \item mucho — the vague version of the same idea.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TRI-ple}, two beats with the weight on the first. \emph{Tr} and \emph{pl} each run together as one sound. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el triple} — \textquotedblleft{}triple,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}three times as much.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{triplus} is two pieces. \textbf{Tres} is \emph{three}, which you already count with. The \textbf{-plus} on the end is an old root meaning \textbf{fold}.

So \emph{triple} is \emph{threefold} — a cloth creased three times, and therefore three layers thick where it was one.

That fold runs through English in disguise. \textbf{Simple} is \emph{one-fold}, a thing with a single layer. \textbf{Double} is \emph{two-fold}. \textbf{Multiple} is \emph{many-fold}. \textbf{Triplicate} is three copies, three folds of the same paper.

Spanish uses \emph{el triple} as a noun, with \emph{de}: \textbf{el triple de libros}, three times as many books.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to count past your fingers: a hundred, an amount, both, several and three times over.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el triple}
  \item \emph{el triple de libros}
  \item \emph{tres o el triple}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the piece \emph{-plus} mean? (Fold.) And what is \textbf{simple}, word for word? (One-fold, a single layer.)
\end{tcolorbox}
